# On the Peculiar Joy of Being Slightly Lost

I've been thinking lately about how we've systematized almost everything. Maps that know where you are down to six feet. Algorithms that predict what you want before you want it. Turn-by-turn directions that don't just show you the way, but scold you if you deviate. It's efficient, certainly. It's safe. It's also, I think, quietly destructive to something we rarely discuss: the productive confusion of being lost.

There's a specific kind of joy that emerges when you're in an unfamiliar place with no immediate way out. Not genuine danger—I'm not romanticizing being trapped in the woods without supplies. I mean something gentler. The kind of lostness that happens when you take a wrong turn in a city and end up on a street you didn't know existed. When your phone dies and you're navigating by memory and landmarks. When you wander off the marked trail and find a meadow nobody else seemed to know about.

That state of gentle disorientation does something to your brain that GPS cannot replicate. It forces you to pay attention. The curve of a building becomes a landmark. The smell coming from a cafe becomes navigation. You notice things—really notice them—because you're actively trying to construct a mental map rather than passively following a blue line. You become a researcher of your immediate environment rather than a follower of directions.

I wonder if we've lost something important by making lostness obsolete.

When I was nine, my father did something that terrified my mother. He took me into the woods near our house and deliberately didn't tell me which way we came. "We're going to get lost," he said, with a grin that suggested this was somehow festive. "And then we're going to find our way back."

For twenty minutes, I was genuinely anxious. Not afraid, exactly, but alert in a way I'd never been before. Every moss-covered log became a potential landmark. I noticed which direction the sun was traveling. I watched which way the stream flowed (everyone knows streams lead somewhere). My father didn't help much—just walked alongside me while I fumbled through the logic of direction-finding like a medieval navigator. Eventually, I got us home by essentially reversing the turns I remembered, confirming them against the landscape.

I was so proud. More than that, I felt *connected* to the physical world in a way I hadn't before. It wasn't my neighborhood anymore—it was *my* forest, mapped by my own cognition rather than handed to me pre-digested.

Now I think about how different that experience is from what we're training our children to do. Swipe, look at the blue dot, go there. The world becomes a series of nodes on a network rather than something you have to actually *know*. And knowing—true knowledge—requires struggle. It requires the productive discomfort of not immediately understanding something.

This extends beyond navigation, I think. We've engineered lostness out of so much of modern life. Streaming services recommend what you watch next. Social media algorithms decide what you read. Amazon suggests what you buy. We're increasingly smoothed into prefabricated paths through information and experience.

There's something to be said for aimlessness. Real aimlessness, not the Instagram-performance of "taking a spontaneous weekend trip." I mean the kind of boredom that forces you to find your own entertainment. The kind of empty afternoon that leads you down a rabbit hole of unexpected thinking. The kind of bookstore browsing where you find something you'd never have searched for.

Some of my best ideas have come from being slightly lost in conversation. Someone says something that doesn't quite make sense, and instead of moving on, I sit with the confusion for a moment. That moment of confusion is where interesting thinking happens. The moment right before everything resolves into understanding is often where genuine insight lives.

We've trained ourselves to minimize that moment. Google it. Look it up. Get the answer. Confusion is an inefficiency to be corrected rather than a space to inhabit. But inefficiency, I'm beginning to suspect, is where the best parts of life happen.

My most meaningful conversations never go as planned. The best vacations always involve at least one misunderstanding. The most interesting people I know are often the ones who've made significant mistakes, gotten lost, and had to figure things out the hard way. There's a kind of depth to someone who has actually *had* to think rather than just consumed pre-processed thinking.

I'm not advocating for rejecting all technology or information systems. That's naive and impossible now anyway. I'm saying that maybe we should be more suspicious of seamlessness. Maybe we should occasionally turn off the GPS just to remember what it feels like to genuinely navigate. Maybe we should sometimes let boredom run its course instead of immediately filling it with content. Maybe we should defend the right to get lost—intellectually, physically, socially.

Because here's what I think is happening: by removing all friction from the process of finding things out, we're potentially removing something that made us more thoughtful, more observant, more fully present in the world. We're trading depth for efficiency. We're choosing the blue dot over the meadow.

The meadow will still be there, theoretically. But if everyone's following the same GPS-optimized path, nobody will ever stumble into it. It'll just be a quiet place that nobody knows about, which is sad for the meadow and sadder for us.

So maybe this is my argument for intentional lostness. For seeking out situations where you don't immediately know what to do. For reading books without first checking what they're about. For taking routes without knowing where they lead. For having conversations that meander instead of arriving at predetermined conclusions.

Not because efficiency is evil. But because the good life—the fully alive life—isn't actually that efficient. It's full of detours and dead ends and unexpected discoveries. It requires the kind of attention that only emerges when you're slightly confused, slightly lost, and forced to pay closer attention to find your way.

And honestly? That state of productive confusion might be the most human thing we have left to protect.
